Captain John Thomas Brady and Charles Edward Parker stood out against Revere. Gibson and Parker were singled out against Winthrop. Beverly scored all 16 points in the first half of its Oct. 10 win on the common. Saugus held Beverly scoreless in the second half, when Beverly used mostly substitutes. On Thanksgiving, Saugus and Stoneham played to a scoreless tie on a field the report described as being in poor condition. The report singled out Libby, Parker and the halfback it identified as Finley. Across the surviving lineups, Brady played left end and left halfback, Parker played fullback and left halfback, and Gibson played right end and fullback. Other names include Burnham, Gammons, Hatch, Hulen, Kinley, Libby, Russell, Weeks and Whittredge. Harry Gibson, named in the 1909 town report, is a possible match for the player listed as Gibson in the 1906 and 1907 lineups.

After Malden postponed its game, Saugus moved up its return meeting with Winthrop and opened its home schedule at Stackpole’s Field on Oct. 24. More than 100 spectators turned out for the 0–0 tie. The Item reported that Saugus gained more than 75 yards on successive line plays in the second half but turned the ball over on downs within two yards of the goal with about a minute left.

Saugus and Burdett College of Lynn played a scoreless 20-minute half at Stackpole’s Field after Burdett arrived late. Saugus stopped Burdett less than a yard from the goal line and had the ball within 10 yards of Burdett’s goal when play ended. The report praised Gammons’s punting and noted that Brady blocked a punt by Burdett’s Tarbox. It also recalled Saugus’s earlier 5–0 win on the same field, which Burdett protested. The rematch lineup lists Knight and Brady at left end.

A second account of the Thanksgiving tie puts the game at Stoneham and reports that about 100 Saugus supporters rode a special car from Monument Square. Saugus drove within a few yards of the goal before a drop kick failed in heavy wind and snow. The report says Saugus kept the ball in Stoneham territory for most of the game and singled out Brady and Parker for Saugus and Grant for Stoneham.

A contemporary newspaper column titled School Football Notes reported that Saugus High fielded a team in 1914 for the first time in several years. The report helps explain the gap in the surviving season records and announced an opening game at Swampscott High. On Oct. 21, Saugus lost 41–0 to Marblehead at Seaside Park. Marblehead halfback Cole scored four touchdowns. The Saugus lineup lists J. Flynn at center, C. Flynn at quarterback, Garofano at right halfback and Fox at fullback. On Nov. 9, Williams scored Saugus’s touchdown against Watertown. Saugus led 6–3 late in the fourth quarter when the referee blew the play dead during a long run by Watertown’s Kinchla, ruling that a player had moved before the snap. Watertown disputed the call and declined to continue. At Needham on Thanksgiving morning, Saugus lost 38–6. Michael Garofano scored Saugus’s touchdown, and the report describes both teams making frequent use of the forward pass.

On Oct. 28, Saugus beat Ipswich Manning High 14–0, with both touchdowns coming in the final period. George Sprague and Gordon Williams scored and Philip Hull kicked both extra points. The Oct. 29 Daily Evening Item called it Saugus High’s first win in six years and reported a torchlight parade. The team photo caption identifies Lupton Reddish as manager and says Carl Lundholm broke his collarbone against Marblehead. The Watertown report records that Watertown argued its player had been moving toward his own goal line, which it said was legal. An undated Cliftondale preview describes Bernard Boyle leading a two-hour practice at Stackpole’s Field and a silver cup offered to the winner. It names Charles X. Flynn at left end and John Flynn at quarterback in the practice lineup. The clipping itself does not establish the season.

seasons.seasonNote:
On March 20, team manager Carl Lundholm announced a preseason schedule. It listed home dates against Revere (Sept. 25), Ipswich (Oct. 9), Winchester (Oct. 12), Swampscott (Oct. 18), the alumni (Oct. 22) and Dedham (Nov. 1), and trips to Lexington (Oct. 1), Winchester (Nov. 6) and Ipswich (Nov. 13). Thanksgiving (Nov. 25) was listed as an open home date in March. A Thanksgiving morning preview later listed Saugus at Needham. The March dates for Ipswich are tentative, and a contemporary box score documents the Dedham game on Oct. 20.

Captain Michael Garofano scored against Winchester on Oct. 12 and twice in the muddy win over Dedham. Smith also scored against Winchester, and Howe kicked the extra point. The box score lists Lundholm at right end. Fullback Fox and quarterback John Flynn scored in the 12–10 win over East Boston. The report singled out Flynn’s runs around the ends. The fourth quarter began after dusk, and East Boston had the ball at the Saugus 5-yard line when time ran out. Flynn also drew praise in the 18–0 loss at Winchester’s Manchester Field. A Dec. 9 report says an injury against Winchester kept him out of the last two games and confirms that he was elected captain for 1916.

Revere scored a touchdown and kicked the extra point before a fight involving players and spectators stopped the Sept. 25 opener in the first quarter. Revere declined to continue. Later coverage reported a 1–0 forfeit in Saugus’s favor. A neutral-site rematch was discussed for Nov. 27, and Saugus challenged Swampscott to a Dec. 2 game for Greater Lynn honors. Swampscott planned to end its season on Thanksgiving. Neither proposed matchup has a documented result.

The six completed games with known scores account for 83 Saugus points and 54 allowed.

The Sept. 27 Daily Evening Item reported that officials awarded Saugus the Revere game 1–0 after Revere refused to continue. In the 20–13 win over Ipswich, Reddish, Garofano and Smith scored and Hull kicked two extra points. In the 13–6 game against the alumni at Stackpole’s Field, Garofano and Allen scored for the high school and Hull kicked an extra point. The alumni borrowed two high school substitutes to fill out their lineup. A postseason report said the school planned to hang an enlarged, framed team photo in its assembly hall and identified Flynn as the next captain.

seasons.seasonNote:
Edward Collier opened practice Sept. 19 with 30 candidates. A Sept. 22 report counted about 20 at practice, only six with proper equipment. Local residents asked the School Committee to help pay for uniforms and shoes. Charles Linehan and Rindge Technical quarterback Ralph Creelman assisted Collier. The contemporary reports identify Collier as coach, superseding the workbook attribution to Charles T. Senay.

Wilson and Michael Garofano scored in the 12–0 win over Cambridge Latin’s second team at Stackpole’s Field on Sept. 30. A separate school football roundup also recorded Brighton’s loss to Saugus. Saugus used the forward pass repeatedly in the 19–0 win against Brighton on Oct. 12. Garofano, George Sprague and Smith scored touchdowns, and Garofano kicked the extra point.

Winchester won 14–6 at Stackpole’s Field on Nov. 4. Garofano scored for Saugus, and the last period was played in darkness. A scheduling mix-up prevented the Nov. 11 Woburn High game. The Saugus High School Independents beat Dorchester Art School in a separate game that day. Another notice reported that Saugus canceled against Winthrop. At Wood Island Park, the paper reported that Saugus failed to appear for a scheduled game at East Boston, where more than 600 spectators had gathered. The clipping gives no awarded score. In a separate 6–0 loss at Chelsea’s Carter Street Grounds, Chelsea stopped Saugus at the 3-yard line and won on Broomfield’s 15-yard touchdown run in the final period. The account singled out Flynn and Garofano for Saugus.

After an earlier notice invited a small high school to play at Saugus on Thanksgiving, the team beat East Boston High 39–7 on Nov. 30. Garofano scored three touchdowns and kicked three extra points. Penney, Flynn and Carlton each scored a touchdown. The undated Dedham clipping remains unassigned.

On Dec. 9 at Ocean Park in Lynn, Harry Dame’s All-Stars defeated Brackett’s All-Stars 14–6 in a postseason game drawing players from Saugus, Marblehead and Lynn. Michael Garofano (right halfback), Wilson (fullback) and Fox (right guard) appear in Brackett’s lineup and match the Saugus season reports. The game account singled out Garofano for his play. This mixed-school game is separate from Saugus’s season record.

Saugus High’s players unanimously elected Michael Garofano captain for 1917. The newspaper reported that he had captained the team as a freshman and sophomore and that a senior rule kept him from holding the captaincy in 1916.

Fred Beresford coached the Warriors, with George Nicholson as captain. Franklin Pike scored in the second quarter at Malden on Sept. 28. Malden sent in its first team late in the fourth quarter and scored twice to win 14–6. Boston High School of Commerce won 32–0 at Brookline Field. Saugus recovered a fumble at the Commerce 15 in the second quarter but turned the ball over on downs.

On Oct. 14, Dedham led 7–6 at halftime at Stackpole Field after Pike scored for Saugus. Dedham withdrew after objecting to Saugus’s physical play, and referee Michael Garofano awarded Saugus a 1–0 forfeit win. Saugus and Melrose tied 0–0 at Messinger’s Meadows on Oct. 29, with both lines drawing praise for their defense.

Pike returned a punt 55 yards for the only touchdown in a 6–0 win over Methuen at Pelham Street Playstead on Nov. 11. A separate scoreboard records a 20–16 win over Manchester, Massachusetts. The clipped scoreboard gives no game date.

Saugus beat Rockland 16–6 in postseason play at Little River Grounds in Lynn on Nov. 25. Edward “Googie” Amery caught a first-quarter touchdown pass and ran 32 yards after the catch. Pike scored on a 75-yard interception return in the third quarter, as identified by the Lynn Item. Kelley kicked both extra points. A second account says a high snap by Rockland’s McQuaid led to the safety and credits Saugus guard Joseph Maddocks with helping force it. The account also praises center Raymond Saxon and says Rockland’s only touchdown came when McClure ran back a fumble.

The newspaper’s 1921 football letter list named Amery, Roy Andrews, Henry Bradford, Harold Calderwood, Harold Davis, Charles Emerson, Edwin Holmes, Raymond Kelley, Joseph Maddocks, George Herald, Forest Kenerson, George Nicholson, Franklin Pike, Raymond Saxon, Ernest Littlefield, and John Poole. The clipping identifies Amery as captain-elect for the following season and prints his first name as Edwin. Other season sources identify the 1922 captain as Edward “Googie” Amery. The clipping also repeats the surname Davis on the football list.

The local Dedham account identifies the game as Saugus’s home opener. It describes Pike running more than half the field for his touchdown and singles out right end Holmes and tackle Kelley on defense.

Two Lynn Item Gridiron Gossip columns trace Pike’s emergence as a first-year fullback. One praised his play against Malden and in a separate meeting with Danvers. The Danvers reference gives no score. In the column previewing the October 29 Harvard–Centre game, the Item praised Pike’s work on offense and defense and singled out Pike and Kenerson as two of Beresford’s standouts.

seasons.seasonNote:
Fred Beresford’s Warriors finished 9–0–2, the school’s first unbeaten football season according to a contemporary roundup. The same roundup names Marblehead and Lynn Classical as joint North Shore League champions. The early schedule notice recorded a scrimmage with Lynn Classical at Stackpole Field, where tackle March and end O’Neil drew attention. After a 7–7 opening tie with Swampscott, Saugus won six straight. The Daily Evening Item described a light team that used a shift to set up its end runs. The postseason recap reports that only about 30 candidates turned out and that injuries exposed the lack of experienced reserves. The Item put the team’s average weight at 142 pounds and described Pike as a runner, passer and drop-kicker in Beresford’s open offense.

Danvers visited on October 7 for the home opener. An October 24 report said the Danvers coach withdrew his team with Saugus leading 7–0. The referee awarded Saugus a 1–0 forfeit, which Beresford declined to accept. The 11-game postseason table uses 1–0, while two other newspaper roundups list the 7–0 score on the field.

At Methuen’s Pelham Street Playstead on October 12, fullback Franklin “Ooze” Pike scored both Saugus touchdowns in a 14–7 win, opening the scoring on a 65-yard first-quarter run. Captain Edward “Googie” Amery added both extra points. On October 21, with about a minute left in a scoreless home game against Wellesley, Amery broke a 95-yard run and Pike carried the ball over for a 6–0 win.

Saugus shut out Somersworth, New Hampshire, 32–0. On November 18 it held a much larger Coburn Classical Institute team from Waterville, Maine, to a 0–0 tie before a reported 7,000 spectators at Stackpole Field. The game report highlighted the punting, and the Globe grouped Saugus with Winchester and Norwood among Greater Boston’s standout small-school teams. Albert J. Woodlock also named Saugus among teams unbeaten against Massachusetts opponents. The postseason account reports that Coburn had also tied Colby’s second team, beaten Maine’s second team and lost narrowly to the Dartmouth freshmen.

The year-end score table records a 52–7 win over Braintree and a 24–6 victory at Danvers on Thanksgiving, November 30. The latter was played in the mud two days before the finale. The November rematch followed the October forfeit.

On December 2, Saugus beat Woburn 20–9 at Stackpole Field before nearly 2,000 spectators. John O’Neil recovered a punt touched by Woburn, and a pass from Kenerson to Pool helped set up Amery’s opening touchdown. Pike scored on fourth down on the next Saugus scoring drive, and Amery kicked the extra point. Pike later broke a 60-yard run before being tackled, sprained his ankle and briefly left the game. Amery intercepted a pass and returned it to midfield before halftime. Woburn closed to 13–9, then Pike scored again in the fourth quarter and Amery kicked his second extra point. Kenerson was injured on a late passing play and left the game.

The December recap lists O’Neil and George Nicholson at end, Edwin Holmes and S. H. Pike at tackle, George “Podge” Herald and Willis Dean at guard, Arthur Goodhue at center, Amery and Lester Pool at halfback, Franklin Pike at fullback and Forrest Kenerson at quarterback. The in-season feature describes Pool as a speedy open-field runner and sure tackler and Amery as the team’s leading punter. It also highlights Melvin March and Sidney Pike competing at left tackle, Abraham Pinciss’s defense at right tackle, and Henry Bradford’s receiving and tackling at end. School authorities and most supporters favored ending the season after Woburn despite interest in postseason games. The December 11 recap identifies the regular eleven in its team photograph and reports large home crowds and strong traveling support. It also describes difficulty booking games with other North Shore high schools.

The archive lists Saugus as Greater Lynn League champion. Beresford said during the season that the team was claiming no title at that point, when Waite High of Toledo, Ohio, approached him about a possible intersectional game. The Item’s roundup had Saugus at 6–0–1 through the Somersworth win, with 127 points scored and 17 allowed. That midseason tally uses the roundup’s 7–0 scores for Danvers and Wellesley. The 1942 Tontoquonian later referred to a 1922 Class C championship.

Scoring summary: The listed game results total 216 points for Saugus and 39 against, including a 1–0 administrative forfeit against Danvers. These are schedule-entry totals, not an all-on-field scoring total.

seasons.seasonNote:
Charles “Buzz” Harvey’s team won the North Shore championship and placed second in the state Class C standings, according to the town report. Co-captains Stan Green and Jim Duffy led a team that recovered from a 12–0 opening loss to Medford and went unbeaten over its final ten games. The yearbook results include seven shutouts, a 3–0 win over Salem and a 38–6 Thanksgiving win over Danvers.

A preseason clipping described Harvey’s squad as small and identified Green at end and Duffy at guard. Tackle Pitman and halfback Harrington were among the returning veterans. Back Pratt and center Riley drew attention in practice after seeing reserve duty the previous fall.

The 21–0 win over Amesbury handed the previously unbeaten team its first loss and marked the first points it had allowed. The press called Saugus a dark-horse Class C contender ahead of the Wakefield game. Later reports placed the Sachems fourth after Needham’s first loss, third entering the Swampscott game after North Quincy fell to Norwood, and second after Saugus beat Swampscott 20–0. A 40–0 win over Marblehead pulled Saugus closer to first-place New Bedford Vocational.

Saugus added a home game against Class A Salem before its Thanksgiving date with Danvers. Contemporary coverage laid out a path to first in Class C if Saugus won both games and New Bedford Vocational lost to New Bedford High. The Schoolboy Sidelights column singled out the newly booked Salem matchup as the leading game on a quiet Saturday schedule. Seating nearly derailed the game before the Saugus Park Department agreed to add about 2,000 seats, bringing estimated capacity to about 7,500. In his preview, Ernest Dalton identified Stackpole Field as the venue and pointed to the strength of Harvey and assistant Nick Morris’s line. Joseph Bucchiere kicked the decisive field goal in the 3–0 win, with Harrington holding.

Saugus closed at home with a 38–6 Thanksgiving win over Danvers. The Sachems led 7–6 after the first quarter and scored the game’s final 31 points. Harrington scored two touchdowns, and Eddie Shipulski, Pratt, Allen and Stan Green scored one apiece. Bucchiere kicked two extra points. The win secured second place in Class C with a 6.44 rating behind undefeated New Bedford Vocational at 6.86. Co-captains Duffy and Green spoke for the team; the squad received gifts, the coaches were appointed honorary policemen by Chief John Stuart, and Cunningham showed Rose Bowl pictures.

Lettermen elected Mike Harrington and George Flaherty as 1940 co-captains. Harrington had been a backfield regular for three years, alternating at quarterback and halfback; Flaherty was a regular guard in 1939 with experience the previous season.

seasons.seasonNote:
First-year head coach Henry “Toz” Toczylowski and assistant Edward Galligan installed a new system and led Saugus to an unbeaten Class C state championship. Before the opener, Globe columnist Harold Kaese reported that Toczylowski turned down a $6,200 offer from the NFL’s Brooklyn Dodgers and honored his $2,200 agreement to coach football and teach English at Saugus High. Halfback John “Iron Mike” Harrington and tackle Dick Macdonald were co-captains. Ernest Dalton’s preseason Boston Globe report counted five returning starters, including both captains. It projected Harrington and Eddie Shipulski at halfback, Tommy Atkins at quarterback, Welcome Goss at fullback, and Art Statuto at center.

On September 12, nearly 7,000 watched the Sachems open under the lights at Stackpole Field with a 32–0 win over Chelsea. Shipulski scored on runs of 49 and 11 yards and threw a touchdown pass to Bob Nadeau. Harrington ran 18 yards for a score and threw a 35-yard touchdown pass to Tommy Atkins. Bob Connell kicked both extra points. Chelsea crossed midfield twice and never reached the Saugus 40. Saugus then shut out Woburn 13–0. Each opening win earned eight standings points, and the Globe’s weekly roundup highlighted both Harrington and Shipulski. Harrington’s touchdown in the final minute salvaged a 6–6 tie with Class A Leominster. Shipulski and Harrington broke touchdown runs of 70 and 37 yards against Gloucester in a 14–7 win. Shipulski added a 57-yard touchdown run in the 34–0 win over Amesbury.

The Sachems shut out previously unbeaten Melrose 13–0 and defeated Revere 26–0 on Monday night, November 3, at Paul Revere Stadium after rain postponed the Saturday game. Harrington and Shipulski scored two touchdowns apiece and Bob Connell kicked two extra points. Saugus led 12–0 after three quarters and scored twice in the fourth. The yearbook singled out center Art Statuto for his defensive play against both the run and the pass in the Revere shutout. In the 34–13 win over Swampscott, the yearbook credits Shipulski and Harrington with touchdown runs of 87 and 47 yards. Holbrook’s postseason account gives those runs as 88 and 55 yards. Harrington threw to Claude Collette for the only touchdown in a 6–0 win over Marblehead.

The Globe’s weekly ratings show how Saugus pulled ahead in Class C. Saugus and Winchester shared the early lead going into the Gloucester game. After the Amesbury win, Saugus had outscored its first five opponents 99–13 and was tied with Marlboro at 7.00. The win at Melrose, then the Class B leader, earned Saugus eight standings points and moved it into sole possession of first at 7.17. Saugus was idle the following weekend, and its lead grew when Marlboro tied Wellesley. The Revere win brought Saugus to 51 standings points through seven games, a 7.29 average. After the Swampscott win, Saugus led Attleboro 7.13 to 6.00 with Marblehead and Wakefield left to play.

Saugus had already clinched Class C before Thanksgiving. The win over Wakefield added eight standings points and raised Saugus’s final rating to 7.30, a figure that would have ranked third among Class A teams, behind Lynn Classical and Salem. Unbeaten, untied Attleboro finished second in Class C at 6.00, followed by Winchester and Danvers.

Shipulski led the team with 84 points entering Thanksgiving, but an elbow injury kept him out of the starting backfield. Russ Babcock started at halfback alongside Harrington. After a scoreless first half before a reported 10,000 at Stackpole Field, Welcome Goss scored from one yard in the third quarter and from three yards in the fourth. Harrington helped set up both touchdowns, and Shipulski contributed to the second drive. Wakefield’s Larry Bartnick threw a touchdown pass to Red Czarnota in the closing seconds. Saugus won 12–6. The Globe and yearbook agree on 12–6. A later rivalry table lists 13–6.

In Robert Holbrook’s postseason interview, Toczylowski credited the championship to team balance. He singled out Harrington as a triple-threat back and Shipulski as the fastest player on the squad, highlighting Shipulski’s performance against Melrose and Harrington’s late score against Leominster. He also praised Atkins’s blocking and Larry Daniels’s play at guard. Atkins lined up at quarterback while Harrington called signals.

Harrington made the Boston Globe’s All-Scholastic second team at back and its North Shore All-Scholastic eleven. Globe honorable mentions went to ends Claude Collette and Stanley Wladkowski, tackles Dick Macdonald and Doo Pendlebury, guards Larry Daniels and Lennie Flaherty, center Art Statuto, and backs Welcome Goss and Eddie Shipulski.

The ten documented results add up to 190 points scored and 32 allowed, with six shutouts. Swampscott was the only opponent to score more than one touchdown. Superintendent Vernon W. Evans recognized the Class C championship in his year-end town report and commended both Toczylowski and Galligan. A newspaper clipping also records plans for a Town Hall banquet honoring the unbeaten team and an educational trip to New York, Washington and Annapolis.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas, a former Boston College tackle, took over from Dave Lucey in the spring. George Laskey’s running stood out in a spring scrimmage against Lowell, and the report credited center Alan Speak and guard Dan Murphy for controlling the middle. Tom Sheehan, Mike Harrington, Alan Campbell and Andy Forti helped throughout spring practice, with Art Spinney and John Quinlan also lending a hand. Janusas installed the T formation. Gene Mack Jr. identified left end Eddie Ayers as the leading receiver, with Art Rowe and Bill Calhoun returning on the line and Frank Forti at fullback. Anganis doubled as a punter, and sophomore Sardi Nicolo pushed him for time at left halfback. Saugus was outweighed in each of its first four games and still opened 3–1. Captain Ernie Anganis, quarterback Earl Dudman and tackle Eugene Decereau gave Janusas experienced players around Laskey. Saugus played independently in 1947. The Globe reported the school’s readmission to the Northeastern Conference the following October.

Brookline won its 17th straight game in the 12–6 opener. Anganis recovered a fumble in the end zone for Saugus’s touchdown. Laskey intercepted a pass and returned it 12 yards, then had an 80-yard kickoff-return touchdown called back for clipping. His 27-yard reception helped get Saugus to the three, and the Sachems were a foot from the goal line when time expired. Janusas earned his first win the next week, 7–0 before a reported 7,000 at Beverly’s Hurd Stadium. Two Anganis completions to Ayers gained 42 yards. Laskey’s 16-yard catch and four-yard run set up Anganis’s two-yard touchdown, and Decereau kicked the extra point.

Trailing Chelsea 13–0 in the third quarter, Saugus got a spark from Laskey’s 45-yard kickoff return and 30-yard reverse. Anganis threw to Frank Forti for the first Sachem touchdown. Decereau recovered a fumble at the nine, and Laskey scored on the next play to help put Saugus ahead. Center Alan Speak intercepted a pass and returned it 28 yards to the Chelsea 19. Anganis found Ayers for 16 yards during the ensuing drive, then scored from the three, and Decereau kicked all three extra points in the 21–13 win. Against Amesbury, Laskey ran for 102 yards on 13 carries before a reported 5,000 at Stackpole Field. He caught a pass from Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo and ran the final 30 yards of the 60-yard scoring play, then added an eight-yard touchdown run in the 14–6 win.

Anganis capped the opening 56-yard drive against Revere with a 24-yard touchdown run. Saugus trailed 7–6 at halftime. Dudman found Laskey for a first down and Anganis for 27 yards before Forti finished the 57-yard winning drive from the one. The 13–7 win was followed by a 14–0 shutout of Lynn English before a reported 12,000 at Manning Bowl. Saugus led 16–3 in first downs and 278–34 in rushing yards. Art Rowe recovered a fumble to start the first scoring drive, and a long Anganis run with a lateral to Forti set up the score. Saugus intercepted two passes. Dudman scored from the one on a sneak and Anganis found Laskey for a 20-yard touchdown. The win ended English’s 11-game unbeaten run, gave Saugus five straight wins and lifted the Sachems from fifth to first in the Class B ratings at 6.67.

The streak ended in a 20–7 loss to Lynn Classical before a reported 18,000 at Manning Bowl. Dan Murphy and Ed Falasca blocked a quick kick that Jim Burns recovered at the Classical 20. Anganis threw to Dudman for a touchdown, and Decereau’s kick made it 7–0. Classical tied it by halftime and added two second-half touchdowns. The Globe preview focused on cousins Ernie Anganis and Harry Agganis. Against Swampscott, Anganis left with a recurring knee injury, and Laskey scored twice on the ground in a 20–0 shutout. Dudman returned a punt 86 yards to the two and scored on the next play. With Laskey and Anganis sidelined against Marblehead, Nicolo and Fred Quinlan helped Saugus win 14–6. Ed Ayers blocked a punt, a Nicolo completion set up a Dudman sneak, and Quinlan broke a long touchdown run before halftime.

Saugus entered Thanksgiving needing a win over Peabody and losses by both Brookline and Gloucester to take Class B. Peabody led 6–0 at halftime on a one-yard run by Connors. Saugus reached the Peabody 20 in the third quarter before Laskey was injured. Art Drivas caught a deflected touchdown pass in the final minute, and Regis converted to finish the 13–0 win. The Sachems finished 7–3, fifth in Class B at 5.40, with 116 points scored, 77 allowed and three shutouts.

Laskey and Decereau made both the Boston Globe Class B All-Star team and the Lynn Item All-Scholastic team. The Boston Post also identified Laskey as one of its All-Scholastic selections. Laskey won the Thomas R. Atkins Memorial Trophy, and Decereau won the Lawrence P. Daniels Memorial Trophy. Lynn Classical’s George Bullard later called Laskey the best individual player he faced.

Dudman played in the November 29 Massachusetts All-Star team’s 40–0 win over New Hampshire. Laskey was selected for that game and did not play. On December 7 at Manning Bowl, Laskey scored on a two-yard plunge and Decereau kicked an extra point in the North Shore All-Stars’ 19–6 win over Suburban Boston before a reported 12,000. The all-star game falls outside the Saugus season statistics.

Bob Walsh’s rivalry retrospective records Peabody’s 13–0 Thanksgiving shutout.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas coached the Sachems, and guard Ed Falasca captained the team. Saugus dropped its first seven games, then won three of its last four. Four losses came by seven points or fewer. The 11 documented game scores account for 117 Saugus points and 144 opponent points.

Sept. 11 at Salem, L 12–20. Nearly 8,000 saw Saugus complete seven of eight passes for 170 yards at Bertram Field. Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo found Ken Neale for a 69-yard touchdown on Saugus’ first offensive play after Salem scored. Bill Calhoun intercepted a screen pass in the third quarter, setting up a drive that Fred Quinlan finished off tackle. Calhoun’s extra-point try hit the crossbar, leaving Salem ahead 13–12 before Sam Cronis scored the clincher in the fourth.

Sept. 18 vs. Brookline, L 6–7. Saugus led 11–6 in first downs and had a 70-yard drive stopped at the Brookline four. Jim Blunt later scored on a quarterback sneak after an 18-yard Richie Nicolo pass to Neale and short runs by Frank Forti and Sardi. Paul Penda scored for Brookline with 55 seconds left, and John Sheehan kicked the winning point.

Sept. 25 vs. Beverly, L 6–20. At Bertram Field in Salem, Richie Nicolo and Quinlan helped move the ball from the Beverly 45 to the 19. Richie then hit Ted Fredericks for a fourth-down touchdown that tied the game 6–6. Beverly answered on the first snap after the kickoff, and Billy Ransom scored his second touchdown in the third quarter.

Oct. 1 at Lynn Classical, L 0–6. Don Cheever scored the only touchdown at Manning Bowl, and Jim Marano blocked the conversion. Quinlan’s 35-yard punt return helped Saugus reach the Classical nine. The Sachems lost fumbles there and later at the Classical 24.

Oct. 9 at Amesbury, L 13–27. Forti and Quinlan scored in the first half at Landry Stadium, and Hogle added a point after. Amesbury turned an interception and a blocked punt into scoring opportunities and completed six of nine passes for 103 yards.

Oct. 14. The Northeastern Conference voted in Middleton to readmit Saugus in football, baseball and basketball. The school had left the conference in 1939. The report noted that Saugus had recently been classified Class A. Amesbury and Swampscott were already on the 1948 schedule. The Chelsea preview also reported that injuries had limited the Sachems against Amesbury and that Janusas expected Sardi back.

Oct. 16 at Chelsea, L 6–25. Gene Macomber scored three times before about 3,500 at Chelsea Memorial Stadium. Les DeMasi scored from the 10 with 15 seconds left to finish a 36-yard Saugus drive. Chelsea’s victory was its first over Saugus in eight years.

Oct. 22 at Lynn English, L 0–7. Saugus reached the English 26 before halftime ran out at Manning Bowl. A fourth-quarter fumble at the Saugus 22 set up the only score, an eight-yard fourth-down pass from Bob Caulfield to Lou Tsiropoulos, who also converted.

Oct. 30 at Revere, W 20–0. Sardi, Neale and Don Junkins scored, and Hogle converted twice at Paul Revere Stadium. Saugus scored in each of the first three quarters. The 1949 Tontoquonian gives Sardi’s opening touchdown as a 44-yard run. It says Fred Quinlan intercepted a pass before Nicolo’s touchdown throw to Ken Neale and credits Don Junkins with an interception return for the final touchdown.

Nov. 6 vs. Swampscott, W 14–0. The teams were scoreless through three quarters at Stackpole Field. Sardi broke the tie with a 14-yard run to finish a 59-yard drive and later scored from the 12. Hogle added both points after.

Nov. 15 at Marblehead, L 13–19. Forti pinned Marblehead at its three with a punt and later ran 17 yards for a touchdown. Saugus led 13–12 until a late fumble at the Marblehead 35 gave the hosts the ball. Gardner Hamlen hit Dave Bartlett for a 65-yard touchdown with five seconds left. The game story attributes Saugus’ first touchdown, a two-yard run, to Quinlan, while its scoring summary credits Richie Nicolo. The individual totals leave that touchdown unassigned.

Nov. 25 vs. Peabody, W 27–13. More than 3,500 watched at Stackpole Field as Saugus set a series scoring record and posted its highest score of the season. Dan Murphy recovered a fumble at the Peabody 32, and a Charlie Woodell catch helped set up Sardi’s opening touchdown. Sardi threw two touchdown passes to Neale and a fourth-down touchdown pass to Quinlan after Andy Thain deflected it. Sardi also returned a kickoff 27 yards, Richie hit Quinlan for 28 yards, and Forti had runs of 37, 14 and 13 yards. The Item credits Fredericks and Junkins with blocking an extra point together. The Item puts Sardi’s touchdown run at three yards and describes a separate 25-yard run on the final scoring drive. The Globe reports a 19-yard touchdown run. The individual yardage uses the Item play-by-play for that game.

At the postseason banquet, the Saugus Lions Club presented trophies to Sardi Nicolo and Ed Falasca as the team’s outstanding players. The team elected Nicolo and Dan Murphy co-captains for 1949.

Season scoring totals (from the 11 listed games): Saugus scored 117 points and allowed 144.

Bob Walsh’s Thanksgiving preview at Stackpole Field projected Richie Nicolo at quarterback, Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo and Fred Quinlan at halfback and Frank Forti at fullback. Eligibility losses had reduced Saugus’s backfield depth. Walsh called the game a toss-up despite Saugus entering with two wins and Peabody with one.

Tex Austin’s Item photograph shows Peabody’s Andy Thain reaching for Sardi’s pass near the goal line just before the ball got through to Fred Quinlan for the final Saugus touchdown.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas coached Saugus to a 9–1 regular season and a 10–1 finish with the Exchange Bowl victory. Senior halfback Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo and senior guard Dan Murphy were co-captains. The Sachems scored 281 points and allowed 54 in ten regular-season games (288–60 including the bowl). They won their final nine games and shared North Shore honors with Gloucester. Harvey L. Southward named Janusas and Gloucester’s Nate Ross his area coaches of the year.

Sept. 9 · Joyce Jamboree, Manning Bowl. Saugus beat Lawrence 13–0 in a 15-minute preseason exhibition. Richie Nicolo scored on a sneak, Sardi recovered a fumble and later scored on a 20-yard run, and Leo Kane converted. The exhibition is excluded from the standings and player statistics.

Sept. 17 · Brookline, W 26–14. The Sachems broke a two-game losing streak against Brookline on its home field. The newspaper scoring summary credits Sardi with two touchdowns and three interceptions, Richie with a 40-yard touchdown run, Charlie Woodell with a touchdown and Kane with two extra points. The yearbook also credits Woodell with a 35-yard end-around score. The two accounts describe the order and details of the Nicolo touchdowns differently.

Sept. 24 · Beverly, L 15–20. At Manning Bowl, Bill Ransom returned the opening kickoff for a touchdown. Don Banks and Leo Kane then trapped Ransom in the end zone for a safety. A 28-yard Richie Nicolo pass to Ted Frederick helped set up Sardi’s scoring run. Fred Quinlan put Saugus ahead again in the fourth quarter and Kane converted. Officials ruled a disputed pass a Beverly completion after Richie came away with the ball. Beverly regained the lead on a pass to Ransom. This was Saugus’s only loss.

Sept. 30 · Lynn Classical, W 20–7. Saugus led 14–0 at halftime at Manning Bowl. Richie’s 35-yard completion to Frederick set up Quinlan’s first short touchdown. Sardi added a rushing score, Kane kicked both first-half conversions and Quinlan scored again from the 5. The newspaper scoring summary credits Quinlan with two touchdowns and Nicolo with one. The yearbook prose gives the pair to Sardi. The newspaper split reconciles with the published season scoring totals.

Oct. 8 · Amesbury, W 27–0. At Stackpole Field, Sardi scored on runs of 3 and 53 yards. Fred Flaherty’s interception set up the long touchdown. After Richie intercepted another pass, Sardi ran for 39 yards to set up his brother’s score. Richie scored on a sneak, and Sardi’s 30-yard pass to Frederick set up Woodell’s end-around in the more detailed Amesbury report. Kane kicked three extra points. Saugus recorded 309 rushing yards and 44 passing yards as a team. The shorter newspaper account assigns different scorers. The detailed account and the season scoring totals support the two Sardi touchdowns and the Woodell score.

Oct. 15 · Chelsea, W 40–0. Saugus scored two touchdowns in each of the first three quarters at Stackpole Field. Sardi ran for three touchdowns, including a 53-yarder. Richie ran for one and threw scoring passes to Frederick and Woodell. The yearbook credits Kane with two kicks. The newspaper credits D. Murphy with a safety on Chelsea quarterback Rubenstein. The squad roster identifies him as Dan Murphy.

Oct. 21 · Lynn English, W 21–0. Before a reported 10,000 at Manning Bowl, Sardi broke the scoreless tie late in the first half with a punt-return touchdown. He added a rushing touchdown after halftime, and Richie threw a touchdown pass to Quinlan. The game report credits Frederick with catching a conversion and Sardi with running in the other two. The Globe places the punt reception at Saugus’ own 25, which makes it a 75-yard return. The Item and the yearbook give 67 yards. The two newspapers put Sardi’s second touchdown at 18 yards. The yearbook lists 20.

Oct. 29 · Revere, W 53–0. Saugus led just 6–0 at halftime before scoring 47 points after the break. Quinlan had three touchdowns and Sardi two. Tony Serino added a 15-yard run, Woodell caught a Richie Nicolo touchdown pass, and Ken Richards recovered a fumble for the final touchdown. The yearbook identifies the 53 points as a school single-game scoring record at the time.

Nov. 5 · Swampscott, W 28–0. At Blocksidge Field, Richie scored on runs of 6 and 50 yards, Quinlan ran for touchdowns of 10 and 25 yards, and Kane kicked four extra points. Saugus completed a five-game shutout streak during which it outscored opponents 169–0.

Nov. 12 · Marblehead, W 25–7. Saugus broke a scoreless halftime tie when center Jim Marano returned an interception for a touchdown. The yearbook credits Marano with four interceptions that day. Bud DeMaci recovered a fumble before Sardi broke a 69-yard touchdown run on a triple reverse, as measured in the contemporary game account. Quinlan and DeMaci added fourth-quarter rushing scores. The Thanksgiving preview shows 26–7, but the game report and yearbook schedule agree on 25–7.

Nov. 24 · Peabody, W 26–6. Before a reported 7,500 at Stackpole Field, Richie threw two touchdowns to Woodell and Sardi ran for the other two, including one after a recovered kick. The game report and yearbook differ on the order, play lengths and extra-point attribution. Southward’s scoring recap credits Sardi with a rushing extra point and confirms that he finished the regular season with 99 points.

Dec. 3 · Exchange Bowl, Weymouth, W 7–6. Before a reported 10,000 at Manning Bowl, Saugus lost six of seven fumbles. Weymouth, previously undefeated and untied, took a 6–0 fourth-quarter lead when Bill Ahlstedt scored from the 1 after a fumble recovery. With 20 seconds left, Richie evaded the rush and threw a 50-yard touchdown pass to Sardi, who caught it near the 2 and ran it in. Frank Dudman held and Leo Kane kicked the winning extra point. Sardi also intercepted a pass earlier in the game. A postgame column reported that he played most of the game with a double dislocation of his thumb, suffered in the first quarter.

Scoring and honors. Sardi led the North Shore with 16 regular-season touchdowns and three extra points (99 points), followed among Sachems by Quinlan with 10 touchdowns (60 points), Woodell with six touchdowns and a conversion (37 points), and Richie with five touchdowns (30 points). Kane led area kickers with 20 regular-season extra points. The Exchange Bowl raised Sardi to 17 touchdowns and 105 points and Kane to 21 extra points. The Boston Globe picked Sardi at back and Murphy at guard on its Class A All-Star team, separate from its overall All-Scholastic selections. The Lynn Item honored Sardi, Murphy and Quinlan.

Bob Walsh’s rivalry retrospective recalls the 26–6 Thanksgiving win and highlights brothers Sardi and Richie Nicolo in Saugus’s backfield.

In a spring scrimmage against Peabody, about 2,000 spectators saw Saugus use both T and box formations at Stackpole Field. Sardi Nicolo’s passing drew praise, and assistants John Scarborough and Mike Harrington worked with John Janusas. The Thanksgiving preview photographed the seniors ahead of their final home game and framed the holiday meeting as a rubber match after Peabody’s 1947 win and Saugus’s 1948 victory.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas’s Sachems finished 8–2 and repeated as Exchange Bowl champions. They were 7–2 before the bowl and won their final seven games played. The North Shore season included one forfeit loss and one rain cancellation. Using contemporary game reports for Salem and Thanksgiving, Saugus scored 269 points and allowed 75, including the bowl and the 0–6 Beverly forfeit. Co-captains Leo Kane and Ted Frederick led a lineup that featured quarterback Richie Nicolo, halfback Jim Driscoll and end Charlie Woodell.

September 16 · Brookline, W 25–6. With Nicolo recovering from an appendectomy, Driscoll shifted to quarterback. Art Jolly finished the opening 48-yard drive. Driscoll threw two touchdowns to Woodell and completed a 17-yard pass to DeRosa before Frederick scored from the six. Dick Rumson recovered a fumble to set up Woodell’s second touchdown. Kane kicked the final extra point. In Gene Mack Jr.’s follow-up, Janusas praised Driscoll’s work at quarterback and noted that all-scholastic end Ted Frederick volunteered to play halfback with Jack White injured. Janusas expected Nicolo to return for the Lynn Classical game after Beverly.

September 23 · Beverly, L 0–6 by forfeit. Beverly led 6–0 at Manning Bowl when Janusas disputed a completed pass with about three minutes left in the second quarter. Officials penalized Saugus, Janusas withdrew his team, and fighting involving players and spectators stopped play. The referee awarded the game to Beverly, and the District One headmasters’ committee later upheld the decision.

September 30 · Lynn Classical, L 6–7. Frederick scored after a 68-yard Saugus drive. An offside penalty erased Kane’s successful conversion, and Classical stopped the retry. A Saugus fumble near its own goal set up Classical’s touchdown and Joe Cottagio’s deciding extra point.

October 7 · Marblehead, W 14–6. Nicolo completed seven of eight passes. Woodell caught touchdown passes of 48 and 7 yards and added a 54-yard reception to set up the second score. Kane converted twice. Ed McIntire intercepted a pass after an early Saugus fumble, and Driscoll helped stop a Marblehead drive near the goal line.

October 14 · Chelsea, W 41–6. The yearbook credits Nicolo with touchdown runs of 21 and 11 yards and a scoring pass to Woodell. Tony Serino scored on runs of 30 and 3 yards, and Kane returned a blocked kick 33 yards for a touchdown.

October 20 · Lynn English, W 39–0. Driscoll scored from 60, 44 and 22 yards. Center Jim Marano returned an interception 27 yards for a touchdown, Charlie Murphy recovered a fumble that set up Nicolo’s one-yard score, and Kane blocked and returned a kick 10 yards for a touchdown.

October 28 · Revere, W 26–12. Saugus answered an early 12–6 deficit with two touchdown runs by Driscoll, a Nicolo sneak, and two successful conversions. Serino scored the opening touchdown. Saugus had 14 first downs and held Revere without one, with Revere losing two net yards in the second half. Nicolo and Woodell connected twice for reported gains of 17 and 31 yards.

November 4 · Swampscott, canceled. Rain washed out the game, and it was never made up.

November 11 · Salem, W 41–6. Woodell scored four times, with the yearbook identifying three of those scores as Nicolo passes. Driscoll and Jolly scored the other Saugus touchdowns and Kane kicked five extra points. The Globe’s game report and the yearbook narrative agree on 41–6. The yearbook’s schedule table prints 46–7.

November 23 · Peabody, W 47–14 at Stackpole Field. Saugus scored 27 first-quarter points and led 41–0 at halftime. Woodell scored twice. Driscoll, Jolly, Nicolo, Jack White and Charles Horman scored once each, and Kane made five of seven placements. The Globe’s same-day game account identifies both Peabody touchdowns and both extra points. The yearbook narrative gives 47–12 and its schedule table prints 47–0.

December 2 · Brockton, W 30–12 in the Exchange Bowl. Nicolo’s 23-yard completion to Woodell set up his own five-yard touchdown. After Brockton took a 12–7 lead, Nicolo found Woodell for a 38-yard score and then returned an interception 60 yards for a touchdown. His 21-yard pass to Frederick finished the scoring for Saugus, and Kane converted after all four touchdowns. Charlie Murphy and Kane helped hold Brockton to 36 rushing yards. Saugus added a late safety when Brockton recovered its blocked punt in its own end zone.

Honors and statistics. Nicolo and Driscoll made the Lynn Item All-Scholastic team. Both received Boston Globe honorable mention, along with Woodell, Kane and Murphy. Nicolo was named Exchange Bowl MVP and sat out the following day’s North Shore–Suburban All-Star game with a knee injury. Woodell led Saugus with 12 touchdowns, and Driscoll and Nicolo scored seven each. The scoring accounts identify all 40 Saugus touchdowns. Individual yardage, defensive plays and some conversion attributions are available only in part.

Bob Walsh’s rivalry retrospective highlights the Nicolo brothers and prints the Thanksgiving score as 47–13. The contemporary Globe box score documents two successful Peabody extra points, supporting 47–14.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas returned all but one regular from a 1–9 team. Junior quarterback Charlie Lawrence led a deep backfield that included Malcolm “Mal” Rice, Bill Whittredge, Bob Piwowarski, Bill MacNeill and Jack Lawrence. John Leahy and Doug MacNeill co-captained the team, with Tex Scarborough assisting Janusas. Bill MacNeill scored Saugus’s touchdown in the 18–6 preseason Joyce Jamboree loss to Haverhill at Manning Bowl.

Sept. 26 · Saugus 28, Revere 0. About 5,000 watched at Stackpole Field as Rice opened the scoring with a safety and then ran for the first touchdown. Charlie Lawrence threw a touchdown pass to Dave Donaldson and kicked two extra points. Piwowarski and Bill MacNeill also scored. The yearbook credits Whittredge and Piwowarski with fumble recoveries and Lawrence with an interception.

Oct. 2 · Saugus 21, Lynn Classical 0. Doug MacNeill recovered a fumble to set up Piwowarski’s opening touchdown. Whittredge and Bill MacNeill also ran for touchdowns, and Fred Case converted all three extra points. Janusas credited the 5–4 defense with containing quarterback Walter Burns. Bob Belyea anchored the middle, with Leahy and Doug MacNeill on the ends of the five-man front.

Oct. 10 · Saugus 12, Marblehead 12. Marblehead took a 12–0 halftime lead after long interception returns set up touchdowns. Bill MacNeill intercepted a pass for Saugus, and Belyea blocked a third-quarter punt to set up Rice’s 11-yard touchdown run. Charlie Lawrence’s completion to Donaldson opened the fourth-quarter tying drive before Whittredge carried on five straight plays and scored. Marblehead blocked the go-ahead extra-point try.

Oct. 17 · Saugus 14, Beverly 13. The teams resumed their series at neutral Bertram Field in Salem, where Saugus beat Beverly for the first time since 1947. A Bill MacNeill punt pinned Beverly at its one, and the ensuing safety proved to be the margin. The yearbook credits Leahy, Bob Randazzo and Bob Krzywicki on the play. Whittredge’s one-yard run made it 8–0 before Beverly scored twice to lead 13–8. Lawrence found Rice for a 38-yard gain on the winning 77-yard drive, which Piwowarski capped with a five-yard touchdown run in the final minute. Oct. 24 · Saugus 26, Lynn English 18. At Manning Bowl, Lawrence threw a 12-yard touchdown pass to Donaldson. Whittredge and Bill MacNeill scored to help build a 19–6 halftime lead. Lawrence scored the final touchdown, and Whittredge and MacNeill each converted an extra point.

Oct. 31 · Chelsea 13, Saugus 0. Tony Tiro scored both Chelsea touchdowns in the Sachems’ only regular-season defeat. Bill MacNeill’s 40-yard run was the biggest play of Saugus’s main scoring threat, which ended on downs at the Chelsea 10. Nov. 14 · Saugus 27, Salem 0. On Dads’ Day before 2,500 spectators, Bill MacNeill recovered a fumble and later scored from the six. Whittredge added a touchdown and Rice broke a 70-yard scoring run. Nov. 26 · Saugus 33, Peabody 6. Saugus needed a win or tie to clinch the North Shore League title and led 27–0 at halftime at Leo Buckley Stadium. The yearbook also describes a 50-yard Whittredge pass to Donaldson and credits Jack Lawrence and Krzywicki with touchdowns in a different scoring account. The holiday roundup confirmed the league title. Saugus finished 6–1–1 and fifth in the final Class A ratings with 62 rating points and a 7.75 average.

seasons.seasonNote:
John Janusas entered his 13th season with a veteran backfield, a young line and little depth. He planned to build around team speed, with senior quarterback David Russell Mathews and halfbacks Jim Kelleher and Dick Burt returning. Mathews and Kelleher were co-captains. Another senior, David James Matthews, played end.

Saugus opened with a 16–14 win over Revere after trailing by 14. Janusas told Bill Shechman it was the first time in his 13 years at Saugus that his team had come back from that deficit to win. On Oct. 3, the Sachems shut out Lynn Classical 20–0 before about 4,500 fans. Ralph DeFronzo intercepted a pass to set up Kelleher’s 90-yard touchdown run. A blocked kick set up Tim Churchard’s five-yard score, and Kelleher capped a 40-yard drive with a seven-yard touchdown in the fourth quarter. Burt ran for a two-point conversion.

The yearbook records an 18–6 win over Beverly before unbeaten New Bedford handed Saugus its first loss on Oct. 10. The game was scoreless through three quarters before Stan Tenters scored twice in the fourth, the second time after New Bedford recovered a fumble at the Saugus three. A follow-up reported that quarterback Mathews was out.

Saugus beat Lynn English 44–12 on Oct. 23. Burt scored on runs of 20 and 27 yards in the first five minutes and added a third touchdown after halftime. Quarterback Mathews threw two touchdown passes to end Matthews and scored the final touchdown himself. On Oct. 31, Saugus and Swampscott played to a 0–0 tie. Saugus reached the Swampscott 20 in the first half and later stopped Swampscott on downs at the Saugus 19. The tie left the Sachems 4–1–1.

At Brookline on Nov. 14, the Sachems trailed 8–6 at halftime before Brookline scored 22 unanswered points. Mathews’s 18-yard pass to Bucchiere produced the only Saugus touchdown in the 30–6 loss. The report calls the receiver Jim Bucchiere. The yearbook identifies Francis Bucchiere as the team’s end, and the Thanksgiving report calls him Frank.

On Thanksgiving, about 8,500 fans at Stackpole Field saw Saugus defeat Peabody 14–6. Mathews found Frank Bucchiere for a first-quarter touchdown and ran in the two-point conversion. In the fourth quarter, Peabody tried a fourth-down pass from its own 20 and turned the ball over on downs. Burt finished the short drive with a one-yard touchdown run. Kelleher led the Saugus defense, which held Peabody to a late Pete Wahtera touchdown. The win denied Peabody the Class A championship after Brockton tied Weymouth 8–8. Saugus finished 6–2–1 and shared the North Shore League title with Salem.

The Lynn Item chose quarterback Mathews for its first All-Star team and Burt for its second team. The Boston Globe’s Dec. 6 “On the Bench” list recognized quarterback Mathews at back and end Matthews at end. Burt also received the school’s John A. W. Pearce Football Award.

Walter Sheridan’s third Saugus team won its first five games and finished 7–2, scoring 277 points and allowing 74. Seniors Edward Maguire, John Dancewicz and Paul Uga were co-captains. Sheridan brought back a backfield that had played together since its sophomore year, with Christie “Chris” Serino at quarterback, Jim Paolini and Mike Kimball at halfback and Maguire at fullback. The Boston Globe described Saugus as an early Class A contender after its first two wins.

Saugus opened with a 33–6 win over Boston College High. Maguire ran for 150 yards and scored twice, Kimball broke a 72-yard touchdown run and Don Murray scored on a 13-yard pass from Serino and a 65-yard fumble return. In the 36–8 victory over Beverly, Serino’s passing set up three Paolini touchdowns, and Bob Whitehurst recovered a fourth-quarter fumble. The Sachems then beat Lynn Classical 36–19.

Against Marblehead, Al Thurell returned an interception 27 yards for a touchdown on the first play from scrimmage. A Paolini interception set up Maguire’s four-yard score, and Saugus led 16–0 just 3:02 into the game. Paolini added a two-yard touchdown run, and Chuck Shipulski’s fake punt produced an 81-yard touchdown pass to Serino in the 29–0 shutout. A week later, Shipulski intercepted a pass on Lynn English’s first play from scrimmage, setting up the first of Serino’s two touchdowns in a 40–0 win.

Both Saugus and Swampscott entered their Oct. 29 meeting at 5–0. Before an estimated 10,000 at Stackpole Field, Serino scored on a 12-yard rollout and found Murray for a 36-yard touchdown just before halftime. Dick Jauron scored all 13 Swampscott points, including the deciding extra point. Neither team scored in the second half, and Swampscott stopped a late Saugus drive at its 10-yard line to win 13–12.

Saugus rebounded with a 35–14 win at Winthrop. Serino ran for touchdowns of 22 and 20 yards and threw a 25-yard scoring pass to Chuck Bilton as the Sachems built a 29–0 halftime lead. Kimball and Paolini also scored on runs. Against Salem on Nov. 12, Serino’s seven-yard pass to Paolini and Paolini’s conversion catch tied the game 8–8 before halftime. Jimmy Britton’s second touchdown with six minutes left gave Salem a 14–8 win.

On Thanksgiving at Leo Buckley Stadium, Kimball scored on runs of one and 45 yards in the first quarter, and Paolini returned the second-half kickoff 80 yards for a touchdown. Maguire, Dancewicz, Whitehurst and R. Nicolo also scored in the 48–0 win over Peabody, the team’s third shutout. The Lynn Item named six Sachems to its regional All-Star team, and the Globe gave Dancewicz and Maguire All-Scholastic honorable mentions.

Paul Maguire’s Sachems finished 7–2, winning seven games for only the second time in 19 years according to the yearbook. The senior-heavy team carried over three wins from the end of 1968, including an upset of undefeated Peabody, and opened 1969 with five more. Bill Babcock, Richard Conti and John Richard captained the team. Bob Osgood led the passing game, with Greg Manship, Mike Annese and Dan Madden among his targets. Richard and Dan Heaney powered the ground game.

Saugus opened 29–6 over B.C. High before a reported 6,000. Heaney scored on runs of 82 and 61 yards, and Richard rushed for 128 yards and two touchdowns. In the 28–20 win at Beverly’s Hurd Stadium, Osgood hit Manship for 73 yards and helped turn a pass to Richard into an 80-yard touchdown when Richard lateraled to Heaney just before halftime. Osgood found Madden on fourth-and-eight and Annese for the go-ahead touchdown. Heaney sealed the win on a 40-yard run on fourth-and-three, and Richard rushed for 115 yards.

Conti supplied the only points in a 3–0 shutout at Woburn. The game recap credits him with a 44-yard field goal after an offside penalty erased his first make. A later Globe profile lists the kick at 35 yards and describes Conti’s return from a broken leg the previous season. Saugus kept Woburn from reaching midfield in the second half. Lineman John McBride broke his leg in the game. Richard helped carry the offense past Marblehead, 12–7.

Osgood completed six passes for 259 yards and three touchdowns in the 28–26 win over Newburyport. Richard scored on catches of 76 and 43 yards and a two-yard run, then caught a two-point conversion. Heaney’s 11-yard run on a fake field goal set up Richard’s rushing score. Steve Nelson made two key tackles to turn back a Newburyport drive. The Globe’s narrative credits Manship with the decisive 50-yard touchdown catch, while its scoring summary credits Madden.

Swampscott ended Saugus’s eight-game streak with a 27–6 win at Blocksidge Field for its own 24th straight victory. Richard scored from the one, Doug Waybright recovered a fumble and Osgood went 4-for-16 for 91 yards. Saugus rebounded 30–6 against Winthrop at Stackpole Field, rushing for 232 yards. John Nicolo ran for 138 yards and scored from 10 yards out in the 8–6 Northeastern Conference opener at Winthrop. The Sachems scored all 20 points in the first quarter against Lynn English. Steve Desloges caught a 32-yard touchdown from Burt and ran for another score, and Nicolo added a 28-yard touchdown run and finished with 111 yards on 15 carries. At Swampscott, Desloges broke a scoreless tie in the third quarter and Nicolo ran for two fourth-quarter touchdowns in a 19–0 win. Nicolo ran for a touchdown and returned a punt 66 yards for another in the 27–14 win over Lynn Classical. He carried 23 times for 158 yards and added a 22-yard kickoff return. Desloges and Jim Wiswall also scored on the ground, and Spinney caught a two-point pass from Burt.

Burt threw touchdown passes to Tom Heaney and Scuzzarella in the 26–14 win at Danvers, with rushing scores from Desloges and Wiswall. Wiswall scored from the 1 in the 18–7 loss to Salem, and Burt found Scuzzarella for a 35-yard touchdown in the 20–7 loss to Beverly.

On Thanksgiving at Peabody, Desloges scored on a 1-yard run and Burt threw touchdown passes of 25 yards to Wiswall and 40 yards to Scuzzarella. Nicolo ran in a two-point conversion to help build a 20–7 halftime lead. His conversion was his only score that day. Peabody scored twice in the fourth quarter and won 21–20 on Peter Kitsakos’ two-point run.

The ten scoring summaries account for 24 Saugus touchdowns. Nicolo scored nine (eight rushing and one punt return), Desloges six (five rushing and one receiving), Wiswall four (three rushing and one receiving), and Scuzzarella three (all receiving). The Division II scoring table lists Nicolo with nine touchdowns and 54 points. The Thanksgiving box score documents two additional points on his conversion, bringing his total across the ten games to 56. Heaney caught a touchdown and Spinney scored on his interception return. Burt threw six touchdown passes, kicked eight extra points and threw two two-point conversion passes. Nicolo’s Lynn Item profile credits him with 1,110 rushing yards, 378 combined punt- and kickoff-return yards and three interceptions. A preview the following preseason gave him 1,300 rushing yards for 1974. Doug Mackie was named a Boston Globe All-Scholastic as a junior.

Mike Ginolfi’s Sachems finished 9–1 and shared the Northeastern Conference title with Salem. They scored 248 points, allowed 87, posted six shutouts and won their final six games after the 42–6 loss to Swampscott, when Tom Heaney scored Saugus’ only touchdown on a 30-yard run.

Saugus opened with a 35–0 win over Winthrop. John Nicolo threw touchdown passes to Dan Hashem and Frank Scuzzarella, ran 23 yards for another score and kicked three extra points. Against Winthrop, he also rushed for 117 yards on 13 carries, returned a punt 27 yards and intercepted a pass. Nicolo ran for 109 yards and scored both touchdowns in the 14–0 win over Marblehead. At Lynn English, Nicolo, Heaney and Steve Gannon each ran for two touchdowns in a 42–16 win, highlighted by Nicolo’s 66-yard run and Gannon’s 85-yarder.

In the 28–0 shutout at Lynn Classical, Jay LeBranti threw 32- and 85-yard touchdown passes to Scuzzarella, Nicolo scored on a 70-yard run, and Gannon and Mark Calhoun each tackled the punter in the end zone for a safety. Against Danvers, Nicolo scored twice on the ground, threw an 18-yard touchdown to Scuzzarella and kicked a 24-yard field goal in a 30–0 win. He rushed for 160 yards. The cropped box score’s final-score line is unclear, but its scoring plays add to 30.

At Salem, Saugus trailed 14–0 at halftime. John Nicolo scored from the 1 and Tom Heaney caught a two-point pass from Jay LeBranti. Neil Connaughton’s fourth-down sack stopped Salem at the Saugus 20. On the winning 80-yard, 18-play drive, LeBranti found Scuzzarella on third-and-19 with 47 seconds left. The full Daily Item game report gives the touchdown as 25 yards, while the scoring summary lists 20. Nicolo ran for 134 yards on 29 carries and kicked the winning extra point in the 15–14 comeback.

Scuzzarella caught a 31-yard touchdown at Beverly. Nicolo ran for scores of 69 and 12 yards and threw a two-point conversion in the 29–15 win. He ran for 175 yards, including 145 before halftime. At Gloucester, Nicolo scored three rushing touchdowns and kicked an extra point in a 43–0 shutout, taking the Division II scoring lead with 95 points. In his November 25 Thanksgiving preview, the Daily Evening Item’s Bill Abramson reported that starting quarterback Jay LeBranti was doubtful after suffering a bruised kidney in the Gloucester game. Tom Heaney, who had started the first two games at quarterback, was slated to start against Peabody. Ginolfi pointed to the team’s depth, citing Mark Calhoun’s work at fullback after Steve Gannon was injured against Salem. Saugus entered Thanksgiving 8–1 with five shutouts, and Peabody was 6–3 with three straight wins. Saugus still had an outside chance at the Division II Super Bowl.

On Thanksgiving, John Nicolo returned a blocked second-quarter field goal for the only touchdown in the 6–0 Mud Bowl win over Peabody. Bill Abramson’s November 28 Item report says Steve Gannon blocked Joe Silva’s 31-yard attempt and Nicolo returned it 82 yards, with a block from Neil Connaughton. Both coaches credited Gannon in that report. Another contemporary recap credits Doug Mackie and gives the return as 80 yards; Bob Walsh’s later cartoon gives 85. The same leaders table credited Scuzzarella with five touchdown catches, while the game summaries document six. The game summaries also document six rushing touchdowns for Heaney.

In junior varsity play after the varsity comeback at Salem, quarterback George Nicolo threw four touchdown passes in a 26–8 win over Salem. He hit Frank Serino from 60 and 20 yards and Keith Manning twice from 10 yards. George was varsity halfback John Nicolo’s cousin.

Salem handed them their only loss, 7–6 on October 15, when Chuck Sawulski caught a late touchdown pass from Scott Garabedian and Bob Carter kicked the deciding point. Saugus won its final five games. The ten game summaries account for 204 Saugus points and 88 allowed.

Saugus scored twice in the second quarter and converted both two-point tries to beat Winthrop 16–12. Frank Serino caught five George Nicolo passes for 58 yards and three touchdowns in the 25–7 win over Swampscott, earning Boston Globe Division 2 weekly offensive honorable mention. Dan Hashem added an 18-yard scoring run. In its third straight win, a 12–0 shutout of defending Division 3 Super Bowl champion Lynn Classical, the Sachems held Greg Meehan and the Classical running game in check. Nicolo ran for one score and threw to Serino for the other. Paul Nigro scored three times against Danvers, twice on the ground and once on a pass from Nicolo. John Coffey threw an 18-yard touchdown to Tim Fawcett in the 41–6 win and a 28-yard touchdown to Serino in the loss at Salem.

Nicolo threw four touchdown passes at Beverly, two each to Coffey and Serino, in a 28–14 win. Coffey returned a punt 51 yards for a touchdown in the 27–6 win at Gloucester, caught all three Saugus touchdowns in an 18–12 win over Marblehead, and scored on a 34-yard run and a 39-yard catch at Lynn English. Nigro opened the scoring at Lynn English with an 86-yard kickoff return for a touchdown in the 19–14 win.

On Thanksgiving, Tom Dalton’s game report credits Dan Hashem with the opening Saugus touchdown from the 1 after George Nicolo found Paul Nigro to set it up. Earlier coverage credits Nigro with the run. Trailing 10–6 in the fourth quarter, Nicolo, playing with a sore throwing arm, found Frank Serino for the winning touchdown with under five minutes left. Ted Grant’s photo caption and Bob Walsh’s retrospective give 28 yards; Dalton’s game report gives 27. Serino caught six passes for 116 yards and later stopped Keith Wooley short on fourth down to secure the 12–10 win before more than 9,000 at Stackpole Field. The victory reversed the previous Thanksgiving’s 62–6 loss. The November 25 Boston Evening Globe reported that Saugus finished third in Division 2, behind Super Bowl qualifiers Dartmouth and Boston College High.

The Item credited Nicolo with 81 completions in 157 attempts for 1,052 yards. He led the Globe’s Division 2 chart with 15 touchdown passes. Serino led the division with nine touchdown catches and scored 64 points, including five two-point conversions. Coffey was third on the chart with six touchdown catches. The Item credited Coffey with 20 catches for 363 yards. The game summaries document five Nigro rushing touchdowns, one receiving touchdown and one kickoff return touchdown. Mike Ginolfi returned four starters from the 1977 NEC champions: Paul Nigro, Don Trainor, Bill Peach and Mike Allan. Nigro, Trainor and Allan captained the 6–3–1 team. Saugus opened with a 25–0 shutout of Winthrop and a 29–6 win over Lynn Classical. After a 6–0 loss to Danvers, the Sachems beat Salem and Beverly, but consecutive losses to Gloucester and Marblehead ended their bid to repeat.

The Sachems scored 40 first-quarter points in a 46–14 win over Lynn English. Paul Nigro rushed for 271 yards on eight carries, scored on runs of 85 and 86 yards and caught an 83-yard touchdown pass. Sophomore Steve Peach completed all five passes for 241 yards and four touchdowns and kicked four extra points. Ginolfi began substituting in the second quarter. After drawing Swampscott 10–10, the Sachems beat Peabody 30–14 on Thanksgiving, their first win at Peabody in a decade according to the yearbook. The Item’s rivalry retrospective credits Saugus with a 188–11 yardage edge in the second half.

Item All-Stars Nigro, Bill Peach and Steve Peach led the offense. Nigro scored 16 touchdowns, rushed for 1,395 yards and caught 25 passes for 360 yards. Bill caught 22 passes, seven for touchdowns, and intercepted six passes on defense. Steve passed for 1,050 yards and 11 touchdowns and intercepted four passes.

Additional contemporary Boston Globe coverage provides a fuller account of the individual performances. In the 25–0 opening upset of favored Winthrop, senior halfback Paul Nigro, listed at 5-foot-11 and 192 pounds, gained 152 yards on 16 carries and scored three touchdowns, including an 87-yard return of the opening kickoff. Against Beverly, senior tackle Don Trainor made eight unassisted tackles as Saugus held on for a 12–7 win and remained in contention for the NEC lead.

In the 46–14 victory over Lynn English, the Globe described an extraordinary first quarter: Nigro carried eight times for 271 rushing yards, scored on two long runs and an 83-yard reception, and amassed 354 total offensive yards. He had 13 touchdowns for the season at that point. Sophomore quarterback Steve Peach went five-for-five passing for 241 yards and four touchdowns in the opening quarter and converted four extra points. Coach Mike Ginolfi began substituting in the second quarter. The Globe reported that Peach's four touchdown passes covered 55, 83, 42 and nine yards.

Nigro finished his high-school career emphatically on Thanksgiving in a 30–14 victory over Peabody, scoring three touchdowns and rushing for 165 yards, including a 66-yard touchdown run in the third quarter. Peach threw his 11th touchdown pass of the season to John Rouleau and added a 30-yard field goal and three extra-point kicks. Contemporary reports describe Nigro as one of Eastern Massachusetts' leading halfbacks.

Kevin Ward’s final Saugus team finished 8–2 under senior tri-captains Ryan Magnasco, Dan Schena and Chris Mikulski. The ten final scores give Saugus 284 points scored and 128 allowed. At Stackpole Field against Gloucester, Barrett gained 157 yards on 14 carries and scored five times, three in the first quarter. John Cinelli threw three touchdown passes at Marblehead, including an 87-yarder to Mikulski and two to Bill Leahy. Chris Tringale returned an interception 20 yards for a score.

Schena recovered a fumble in the end zone against Salem. Magnasco earned a Gold Helmet against Beverly with 182 yards on 32 carries and four rushing touchdowns, from 4, 4, 14 and 6 yards.

At 8–1, Saugus entered Thanksgiving with an outside chance at the Division 3 Super Bowl. Peabody won 39–8 before a reported crowd of 9,500. A bad punt snap gave Saugus a safety and Magnasco ran three yards for his eighth touchdown. He finished with 583 yards on 125 carries. Magnasco and Schena each recorded more than 100 tackles and made the Item All-Star team. Seven Saugus seniors earned NEC honors, and Schena also made the Division 3 defensive line.

seasons.seasonNote:
Mike Ginolfi’s Sachems opened at Stackpole Field with a 25–0 shutout of Winthrop, ending a 34-game losing streak. Junior L.J. McKanas rushed 29 times for 178 yards and two touchdowns and intercepted a pass. John Plunkett added 71 rushing yards. Mike Mabee opened the scoring with a 6-yard touchdown pass to Derek Bilton, who later added a short touchdown run. Carlo Abate and Dan Wass had 14 and 16 tackles, respectively, as the defense twice stopped Winthrop inside the Saugus 10. Saugus outgained Winthrop 354–116.

Plunkett rushed for 169 yards and scored twice, including a 42-yard run, in a 28–8 home win over Danvers. Bilton ran for two touchdowns at Salem’s Bertram Field, and McKanas sealed the 28–14 win with a 33-yard run in the fourth quarter. Saugus earned its first win over Salem in 20 years and reached No. 16 in the Boston Herald’s Sweet 16. At Beverly, the Sachems erased a 7–0 deficit as McKanas ran for a score and Mike Mayag threw a touchdown pass to Dan Bilton and ran for another, making Saugus 4–0.

Gloucester handed Saugus its first loss, 34–12. McKanas caught a 4-yard touchdown pass from Mabee, who added a 1-yard scoring run. The Sachems rebounded with a 47–6 win over Marblehead. Mabee hit Jamie Sheehan for a 36-yard touchdown, Mike Faiella returned an interception 35 yards for a score, and Ryan Leahy found Sean Rush for the two-point conversion. The box score credits “C.J. McKanas” with 22- and 34-yard touchdown runs. The other reports and the Item’s 11-touchdown figure for L.J. support reading those initials as a listing error.

Saugus secured its first winning season since 1990 with a 50–20 victory over Lynn English at Manning Bowl, its first win over the Bulldogs since 1987. Mabee passed and rushed for 87 yards apiece, threw touchdown passes to Rob Streeter and McKanas, ran for a score and intercepted two passes. McKanas rushed for 149 yards and scored three times, including the 11-yard catch, and Derek Bilton added two touchdowns. The win put Saugus at 6–1.

Swampscott shut out Saugus 18–0, and Mabee suffered a leg fracture. In the 21–6 loss to Lynn Classical, Sheehan threw a 25-yard touchdown pass to McKanas. Mabee returned for Thanksgiving at Stackpole Field as Peabody won the 52nd meeting, 34–14. McKanas helped set up Justin Falite’s 10-yard touchdown run. Abate ran in the two-point conversion and later scored on a 5-yard run. Co-captain Matt Nazzaro, Wass and Derek Bilton left the finale with injuries.

The Item’s postseason profiles credited Mabee with 61 completions in 95 attempts for 720 yards and six touchdowns, 360 rushing yards and seven rushing touchdowns, six interceptions and two fumble recoveries. Abate led Saugus with 115 tackles, four interceptions and four fumble recoveries. Both earned Item and NEC recognition. McKanas was an NEC All-Star and entered Thanksgiving with 680 rushing yards, 1,197 all-purpose yards and 11 touchdowns. The finale coverage documents another run for McKanas, and the scoring summary confirms he finished with 11 touchdowns.

Saugus finished 6–4, scoring 230 points and allowing 162 in ten games.
