history: A Brief History of Saugus High Football
Introduction

At Stackpole Field in 1922, a reported 7,000 spectators watched Saugus play Coburn Classical Institute of Maine to a scoreless tie. In 1941, nearly as many turned out under the lights to see the Sachems open against Chelsea. The town reports preserve what those teams meant to Saugus. The box scores, yearbooks and family scrapbooks preserve something different: who made the tackle, who kicked the point, and how close a championship sometimes came to turning on one play.
1900–1919 (The Early Years):
J.W. Stanley (1901)

The season archive’s earliest listed Saugus High team is the 1901 squad, coached by J. W. Stanley and featuring Charles “Chas” Bennett. A separate 1896 gallery clipping reports a Saugus football team without explicitly identifying it as Saugus High School. Surviving 1906 reports document a partial schedule and identify John Thomas Brady as captain. Contemporary newspaper coverage says the school resumed football in 1914 after several years without a team.

The surviving 1906 results give a partial 1–3–1 record. Captain John Thomas Brady appears at both left end and left halfback, while Charles Edward Parker appears at fullback and halfback. The Thanksgiving meeting with Stoneham ended 0–0.
Arthur L. William (1914)
Arthur L. William coached the returning 1914 team to a 2–7 record. John Fox and George Sprague were among its leading players, and Watertown was the Thanksgiving opponent.
Charles T. Senay (1915)
Senay coached Saugus in 1915. Surviving results include six wins, one by reported forfeit, and an 18–0 loss at Winchester.
Edward Collier (1916–1917)

Contemporary newspaper accounts name Collier as Saugus coach in 1916. He opened practice in September as residents sought help equipping the team. The workbook lists 1916 at 7–1, including a documented 39–7 Thanksgiving win over East Boston. The season records list 1917 at 0–5.
Laurence F. Davis (1919)

The season register lists Davis’s Warriors at 3–6–3. In a 56–6 win over Manning High of Ipswich, Saugus scored 34 points in the first quarter and Bradbury returned an interception 65 yards for a touchdown.
1920–1950: (The Golden Years):

The period from 1920 through 1950 is widely regarded as the “Golden Era” of Saugus football. During that stretch, Saugus won state championships in 1941 and 1944 and Exchange Bowl championships in 1949 and 1950, and produced several other teams that were strong enough to be considered among the best in program history.
Fred Beresford (1920–1922, 1928)

Tim Bannon captained Beresford’s 1920 team, which the season register lists at 5–6–1. Saugus shut out Danvers, Belmont and Manchester in the documented regular-season games. Bannon scored twice against Manchester, and fullback Hilbourne scored in all three wins.

Fred Beresford’s 1922 Warriors finished 9–0–2 behind captain Edward “Googie” Amery and fullback Franklin “Ooze” Pike. Saugus beat Danvers 24–6 on Thanksgiving and closed with a 20–9 win over Woburn. The archive lists the team as Greater Lynn League champions. The 1942 yearbook retrospectively describes a Class C title, while Beresford said during the 1922 season that he was claiming no title at that point.

About 30 candidates turned out in 1922. The Daily Evening Item put the team’s average weight at 142 pounds and described a shifting offense built around Pike’s running, passing and drop-kicking. With about a minute left in a scoreless game against Wellesley, Amery broke a 95-yard run and Pike finished the drive for a 6–0 win.
William Bangs (1923–1925)

William Bangs took over in 1923 and coached through 1925. Bangs maintained competitiveness but did not produce a winning season, finishing 6–6 in his final year. Some notable players on those Bangs teams were Pool and Amery, as well as Ernest Belliveau, Homer McNutt, Wally Gautreau, and Danton Sawyer.

Albion Rice coached in 1926–1927 and returned for 1929–1934 after Fred Beresford’s 1928 season. The archive lists a 7–4 finish in 1927, a 0–9 record in 1928 and a 7–2 season in 1931. The gallery’s 1928 review highlights captain Reggie Goss, Gilman Cann, Carroll Freeman, Red Hunnewell, Stuart Kidder and Jim Foley, including a long Kidder-to-Goss pass in the Thanksgiving loss to Mission High. Its 1929 account records victories over Manchester and Swampscott, while the 1930 pages celebrate captain Jim Muzzy, also spelled Muzzey, and Laurie Templeman. The 1931 season entry names George Riley, Joe Nelson, Malcolm Bisbee, Harry Gates, Red Doherty and Joe Scarozza.
John “Jack” Leahy (1935–1936)

John “Jack” Leahy, a former Saugus captain, coached the 1935 and 1936 teams. The town report confirms seven wins in ten varsity games in 1935. Saugus closed that season with an 18–12 Thanksgiving win over Danvers. The 1936 season archive lists a 2–7–1 finish.

Throughout its history, Saugus has primarily been known as the Sachems, a nickname that began during the Leahy era. Prior to the Sachems nickname and mascot, Saugus used other nicknames including Warriors (1914–1929) and Eagles (1930–1934).
Charles “Buzz” Harvey (1937–1940)

Charles “Buzz” Harvey coached Saugus from 1937 through 1940. His 1939 team finished 9–1–1 and won the North Shore championship, as recalled in the 1942 yearbook and corroborated by the contemporary town report. Co-captains Jimmy Duffy and Stan Green led a team featuring John “Iron Mike” Harrington, Art Statuto, Eddie Shipulski and their teammates. The gallery recounts the 3–0 victory over Salem and the 38–6 Thanksgiving win over Danvers, followed by a celebratory trip to New York and West Point. The town report places Saugus second in Class C; this regional championship should not be described as a verified 1939 state title.

Championship spotlight — 1939: Charles “Buzz” Harvey and assistant Nicholas Morris built a North Shore championship team whose success attracted statewide attention. After an opening loss to Medford, Saugus went unbeaten the rest of the season, including a tie with powerful Melrose and a memorable 3–0 victory over Salem. Weekly newspaper reports tracked Saugus climbing from fourth to second in Class C. After beating Marblehead, the Sachems added a home game against Class A Salem, giving them a chance to finish first if they also beat Danvers and New Bedford Vocational lost to New Bedford High. The 1939 school report credited Saugus as the second-highest-scoring team in Massachusetts and second in the Class C standings among 51 teams. The School Committee celebrated the achievement with a five-day educational trip to New York City.
Henry “Hammering Hank” Toczylowski (1941–1942)
Henry “Hammering Hank” Toczylowski succeeded Buzz Harvey in 1941 after playing quarterback at Boston College under Frank Leahy.

Toczylowski and assistant Edward Galligan guided Saugus to the 1941 Class C state championship. Co-captains John “Iron Mike” Harrington and Dick Macdonald led a team that included Eddie Shipulski, Art Statuto and Eddie Koschei. Harrington earned Boston Globe All-Scholastic second-team and North Shore All-Scholastic recognition. The 1942 Saugus town report records a 7–3–1 season in Toczylowski’s second year.

Championship spotlight — 1941: The 1941 Sachems won the Massachusetts Class C state championship and finished unbeaten. A contemporary Boston Globe retrospective gives 10–0–1. The yearbook schedule and final Class C standings document ten games, and the nine wins and one tie in the surviving results account for all ten. Superintendent Vernon W. Evans recognized coaches Henry Toczylowski and Edward Galligan in the town report.

The opener under the lights was a 32–0 win over Chelsea. Eddie Shipulski scored twice and threw a touchdown pass, and Harrington both ran and passed for a score. Against Class A Leominster, Harrington’s touchdown in the final minute preserved the unbeaten season with a 6–6 tie.
Dave Lucey (1943–1946)

Dave Lucey succeeded Toczylowski in 1943 and coached through 1946. His 1944 team went 10–0 in the regular season and won the Massachusetts Class B championship. Captain Art Spinney earned Boston Globe All-Scholastic first-team honors at end. Doug Waybright captained Saugus in 1943 and graduated in 1944.

Championship spotlight — 1944: Under Dave Lucey, the 1944 Sachems ran through ten regular-season games without a loss to earn the Massachusetts Class B championship. The archive records a dominant 207 points scored and only 19 allowed during that championship run. Art Spinney, Dick Allen, Bob Kane, Don Reiniger, Frank Pyszko and Bruce Waybright were among its standouts. The yearbook also documents a separate 19–7 postseason loss to Class A champion Peabody, which does not erase the team's Class B title. The 1944 town report remembered 1939, 1941 and 1944 as three defining championship seasons.

Eight opponents were shut out. The first points against Saugus came on a 65-yard Newburyport fumble return. A reported 14,000 attended the 24–13 win over Lynn Classical at Manning Bowl, and a 26–0 Thanksgiving victory at Wakefield clinched the title.
1947–1960: (The Janusas Era):
John Janusas (1947–1960)
John Janusas coached Saugus from 1947 through 1960. His teams won consecutive Exchange Bowls in 1949 and 1950, won the North Shore League title in 1953 and shared the league title with Salem in 1959.

John Janusas’s first team went 7–3 in 1947. Captain Ernie Anganis played in a backfield that included George Laskey and Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo. Laskey earned Lynn Item and Boston Post All-Scholastic recognition and made the Globe’s Class B All-Star team. He scored for the North Shore All-Stars in their 19–6 win over Suburban Boston. Saugus finished 3–8 in 1948.

The 1948 team lost its first seven but won three of its last four. At Salem, nearly 8,000 saw Saugus complete seven of eight passes for 170 yards, including Sardi Nicolo’s 69-yard touchdown throw to Ken Neale. Captain Ed Falasca and Nicolo received Lions Club recognition that season.

The 1949 Sachems finished 10–1, sharing the North Shore championship with Gloucester and winning the Exchange Bowl against Weymouth, 7–6. Richie Nicolo’s 50-yard touchdown pass to his brother Sal “Sardi” Nicolo tied the bowl game, and Leo Kane’s extra point secured the victory. Co-captains Sardi Nicolo and Dan Murphy led a team also featuring Fred Quinlan and Richie Nicolo. Southward’s newspaper season wrap-up credits Sardi with an area-leading 99 points and 16 touchdowns and identifies Gloucester as Class B state champion. The ten regular-season results add up to 281 points for Saugus and 54 against, matching Southward’s 281-point scoring tally. The Exchange Bowl brought the totals to 288–60.

Championship spotlight — 1949: An early 20–15 loss to Beverly left Saugus at 1–1. The Sachems won their remaining nine games. Against Amesbury, Sardi Nicolo scored on runs of three and 53 yards and broke a 39-yard run to set up another score. The winning streak carried Saugus from the North Shore schedule to the Exchange Bowl. The superintendent singled out the victory over Weymouth in the town report.

Championship spotlight — 1950: John Janusas’s Sachems won their second consecutive Exchange Bowl, beating Brockton 30–12 on December 2 at Manning Bowl and finishing 8–2. Richie Nicolo ran for a touchdown, returned an interception 60 yards for another and threw touchdown passes to Charlie Woodell and Ted Frederick. Co-captain Leo Kane kicked four extra points and helped Charlie Murphy anchor the line that held Brockton to 36 rushing yards. Woodell led Saugus with 12 touchdowns across the season.
The North Shore title returned to Saugus in 1953. The following fall, co-captains Jack Lawrence and Malcolm “Mal” Rice led the Sachems to a 6–3 finish.

Championship spotlight — 1953: John Janusas guided the 1953 Sachems to a 6–1–1 regular-season record and the North Shore League championship. Co-captains John Leahy and Doug MacNeill led the way, and a commanding 33–6 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody clinched the league crown. The 1954 yearbook explicitly connects that holiday victory to the championship and records the separate Joyce Jamboree loss outside the regular-season total. It was a fitting culmination to another strong season under Janusas.

Championship spotlight — 1959: John Janusas’s Sachems finished 6–2–1 and shared the North Shore League title with Salem, as confirmed by the contemporary School Champions roundup. Co-captains Dave Mathews and Jim Kelleher led a squad that beat Peabody 14–6 on Thanksgiving and ended its Class A title bid.
1961–1972 (Sustaining Competitiveness):
Bernard Stead (1961-1963)

Bernard Stead coached from 1961 through 1963. The season archive records finishes of 0–8, 1–8 and 0–9, respectively, a combined 1–25. Tom Carr is among the notable players listed for that period; the collection does not establish that he was its only All-Star.
Walter Sheridan (1964-1966)

Walter Sheridan coached from 1964 through 1966, culminating in a 7–2 season. The gallery’s 1967 yearbook pages identify the fall 1966 co-captains as Edward Maguire, John Dancewicz and Paul Uga, alongside Christie Serino, James Mancuso, Donald Murray, Richard Lombardo and their teammates. Four pages preserve the squad portrait, named player studies, game photographs, pep squad and cheerleaders.

The 1966 team won its first five games and outscored its opponents 277–74. Against Boston College High, Ed Maguire ran for 150 yards and two scores. Don Murray scored once as a receiver and again on a 65-yard fumble return in the 33–6 win.
Paul Maguire (1967-1972)

Paul Maguire coached from 1967 through 1972. His 1969 Sachems finished 7–2 under captains John Richard, Richard Conti and William Babcock. The yearbook names Bob Osgood and Bill Eichel to the first offensive Northeastern Conference All-Star team and Steve Nelson to the first defensive team, with honorable mentions for Rich Desisto, Babcock, Conti and Richard. The only losses came against Class B champion Swampscott and Class A champion Peabody.
1973–1983: (The Ginolfi Era):
Mike Ginolfi (First tenure 1973-1983)

Mike “Gino” Ginolfi’s first team went 3–6 in 1973. Two of those wins hinted at what was coming. Against Danvers, senior quarterback Richie Serino ran for both fourth-quarter touchdowns, sophomore Steve Gannon made three sacks, and reserve back John Nicolo came off the bench to help set up both scores. On Thanksgiving, Saugus shut out a previously unbeaten Peabody team 12–0. John Nicolo recalled that upset when he coached Saugus against the favored Tanners in 2002. In 1974 the Sachems improved to 6–4. At Winthrop, Nicolo rushed for 138 yards, captain Steve Spinney intercepted two passes, and Mike Burt found Frank Scuzzarella for the two points that decided an 8–6 game.

The 1975 Sachems finished 9–1 and shared the Northeastern Conference championship. Captains Tom Heaney, Doug Mackie, John Nicolo and Steve Gannon led the team. The gallery preserves the 15–14 comeback against Salem and the muddy 6–0 Thanksgiving victory over Peabody. The 1978 yearbook’s review explicitly distinguishes the shared first-place finish in 1975 from the conference title won in 1977.

Championship spotlight — 1975: Saugus shared the NEC title with Salem, the team it had trailed 14–0 at halftime in their head-to-head meeting. Neil Connaughton stopped a Salem drive with a fourth-down sack. On the winning 80-yard, 18-play march, Jay LeBranti found Frank Scuzzarella on third-and-19 with 47 seconds left. The 15–14 win was part of a six-game closing streak. Saugus scored 248 points, allowed 87 and shut out six opponents.
Doug Mackie earned high-school All-American recognition in 1975.

Saugus High’s inaugural 1987 Athletic Hall of Fame class included eight football alumni: Art Spinney, Christie Serino, Doug Mackie, George Laskey, John “Iron Mike” Harrington, John Nicolo, Salvatore “Sardi” Nicolo and Stan Green. The school roster recognizes Dr. John Mangini as an original committee member.

The Sachems followed a 2–8 season in 1976 with a 9–1 Northeastern Conference championship in 1977. The yearbook identifies co-captains Dan Hashem and Frank Doyle and senior contributors including George Nicolo, Frank Serino, Paul Serino, John Coffey and Tim Fawcett. A 12–10 Thanksgiving win over Peabody closed the season. The gallery also preserves Mike Ginolfi’s 1977 Item Coach of the Year recognition.

Championship spotlight — 1977: A 7–6 loss to Salem was the only defeat. George Nicolo threw four touchdown passes at Beverly, two each to John Coffey and Frank Serino. Coffey caught all three Saugus touchdowns in an 18–12 win at Marblehead. The Sachems won their final five, outscored their opponents 204–88 over the season and finished third in Division 2 behind Super Bowl qualifiers Dartmouth and Boston College High.

Four starters returned from the champions in 1978: Paul Nigro, Don Trainor, Bill Peach and Mike Allan. In a 46–14 win over Lynn English, Saugus scored 40 points in the first quarter. Nigro ran for 271 yards on eight carries and caught an 83-yard touchdown pass. Sophomore Steve Peach completed all five of his passes for 241 yards and four touchdowns. The Sachems finished 6–3–1, then went 5–5 in both 1979 and 1980. The 1980 team closed with a 40–6 Thanksgiving win over Peabody.

After going 1–9 in 1981, Mike Ginolfi’s Sachems rebounded to 5–4–1 in 1982. Co-captains Mark Strangie and Anthony Guthro led a team that also featured quarterback Steve Fauci and Anthony Cogliano. Saugus won five straight conference games, finished third in the NEC and outscored its opponents 93–89. The 1983 Sachems went 4–6, led by Tom Trainor, Kevin Pelley and Bob Cinelli.

The 1982 yearbook says the Sachems had been picked to finish last. They shut out Marblehead and Swampscott during the five-game winning streak. Steve Fauci threw eight touchdown passes, including two apiece in victories over Lynn English and Danvers.

Ginolfi would step down after the 1983 season and moved into athletic administration. His coaching tree shaped Saugus football for decades through assistants and former players who followed him into the head coaching role.
1984–1993: Inconsistency and Brief Success
Kevin Ward (1984-1990)

Kevin Ward took over in 1984, and the program went through several down years, though the 1987 team rebounded to go 7-3. Marc Fauci emerged as one of the Sachems greatest players. He was named Boston Globe All Scholastic in 1989.

The 1987 team edged Peabody 21–20 on Thanksgiving. Co-captain Joe Barressi caught nine touchdown passes, ran for two scores and returned two punts for touchdowns. He also kicked and punted, and the Item selected him to its All-Star team at defensive back. Fellow captain Larry Furey earned Item recognition on the offensive line. On Thanksgiving in 1988, Marc Fauci ran for two touchdowns and Steve Worthley caught six passes for 92 yards in a 22–14 win over Peabody, as recorded in Bob Sacco’s Saugus Advertiser illustration. Peabody edged Saugus 14–13 the following Thanksgiving. In Ward’s final season, 1990, the Sachems went 8–2 behind tri-captains Ryan Magnasco, Dan Schena and Chris Mikulski. Justin Barrett scored five touchdowns against Gloucester. The ten final scores give Saugus 284 points and its opponents 128. The Globe called 284 a school scoring record, while the yearbook reported 288.
Mike “Bonty” Bontempo (1991-1993)
Mike “Bonty” Bontempo succeeded Ward and coached from 1991 through 1993. Saugus went 1–29 over those three seasons. Sean Publicover and Joe Attubato earned All-Star recognition during his tenure.
1994–2004: Rebuilding and Setbacks
Mike Ginolfi (Second Tenure 1994-1995)

Mike Ginolfi returned in 1994. After an 0–10 season, the 1995 Sachems snapped a 34-game losing streak with a 25–0 victory over Winthrop and finished 6–4, their first winning season since 1990. Co-captain Mike Mabee, a multi-sport standout, led the team with L.J. McKanas, Carlo Abate, Matt Nazzaro and Derek Bilton. The Newspaper Clippings section preserves the streak-ending game and the 50–20 win over Lynn English that clinched a winning season. An early-season Boston Herald clipping ranked Saugus No. 16 during Saugus’s 3–0 start.

In the streak-breaking opener, McKanas ran for 178 yards and two scores on 29 carries, Plunkett added 71 yards, and Abate stopped Winthrop on fourth-and-one. Saugus followed with victories over Danvers, Salem and Beverly to open 4–0.

Coach Ginolfi retired from coaching after the 1995 season. He will always be remembered as one of the greatest football coaches in Sachem history, as he was a 1993 Saugus High Athletic Hall of Fame inductee, but he was also one of the greatest coaches in Massachusetts Football History as he was inducted into the Massachusetts High School Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame in 1992. Coach Ginolfi would remain Athletic Director at Saugus until he retired from that position in 2002
John Fauci (1996-1998)

John Fauci took over for Coach Ginolfi for the 1996 season. Saugus finished the 1996 season with a 4–7 record. The Sachems were led by John Plunkett, Justin Falite, and LJ McKanas. McKanas would be named to numerous All-Star teams as a RB.

Saugus finished 6–4–1 in 1997 and 5–6 in 1998. The 1998 Thanksgiving preview credits Raphael Zammit with 21 total touchdowns before the finale—18 rushing, two receiving and one interception return—surpassing the previous total-touchdown mark of 20 credited to L.J. McKanas. That total-touchdown distinction should not be confused with a rushing-touchdown record. The same preview highlights quarterback Ryan Leahy, Mike Panzini and their teammates; its figures are pre-Thanksgiving totals rather than confirmed final-season statistics.

In the 1997 opener, Dominic and Raphael Zammit combined for 251 rushing yards against Greater Lawrence. Ryan Leahy also found Raphael for a 50-yard score. In 1998 Raphael ran for five touchdowns at Winthrop and four at Marblehead, where Leahy added two rushing scores. An 82-yard fourth-quarter run by Zammit broke a 14–14 tie at Danvers.
Dean Sacca (1999-2000)

Dean Sacca’s first team opened 1999 with a 6–0 win over Methuen on sophomore quarterback Kyle Sucharewicz’s fourth-quarter run. George Lowe scored three times in a 30–14 win over Marblehead. Against Swampscott he scored on a five-yard run and a 65-yard pass from Sucharewicz. The Sachems reached 3–2 before finishing 3–8. Sacca’s 2000 team, which featured All-Star Ryan Gould, finished 2–8.
John Nicolo (2001-2004)

John Nicolo returned as head coach in 2001. The Sachems went 2–9, but erased a 14–0 deficit at Salem to win 30–14. Kyle Sucharewicz threw three touchdown passes, Dan Landry returned an interception 55 yards for a score, and Saugus put up 24 points in the fourth quarter. On Thanksgiving, Sal Nicolo returned an interception 33 yards for a touchdown and recovered a fumble against Peabody. In 2002 the Sachems finished 1–10. In their 31–16 win over Marblehead, Sal’s 35-yard fumble return set up the first Saugus touchdown.

The 2003 Sachems finished 3–8. Junior running back Mike Nicolo rushed for 1,462 yards and 11 touchdowns and set the then Saugus single-game rushing record with 306 yards against Salem, as documented in the gallery and alumni profile. Anthony “Beave” Barbanti’s senior profile records 75 tackles, 11 tackles for loss and three sacks, alongside his work on the offensive line. Mark Spadafora and Chris Benson also feature in the season entry.
At Beverly the next week, Nicolo carried 37 times for 241 yards and all four Saugus touchdowns in a 29–14 comeback. Rob Gannon threw for one two-point conversion and ran in another.

The 2004 Sachems were plagued with injuries to their core players and the promising rebuild came to a stop as they finished the season 0-11. Nicolo missed part of the season and played most of the season with an injured knee and shoulder. Despite the injuries Nicolo was still named an All-Star along with teammate Brian Bianchi.

The surviving senior-season reports document 429 rushing yards for Nicolo across six games and seven rushing touchdowns across the scoring summaries. The yardage is a partial tally. His longest documented scoring run was 61 yards against Revere in the opener.
After the 2004 season, Coach Nicolo stepped down as Head Coach and took on the role of Athletic Director.
2005–2016: (The Broderick Era)
Mike Broderick (2005-2016)

Mike Broderick took over in 2005 and brought stability back to the program. Coach Broderick was the first Sachems Head Coach to have not been under the Ginolfi Coaching Tree since the Paul Maguire days.

Coach Broderick’s first two seasons were rebuilding seasons for the Sachems. His 2005 team went 1-10, led by All Star Alex Klimarchuk. In 2006 the Sachems improved to 3-7. Although the record didn’t seem like much, this team was remembered for becoming the first Saugus team to defeat the Sachems Thanksgiving Day rival, the Peabody Tanners, for the first time in 18 seasons. That Sachems team was led by senior All Star, Rodney Lavoie. Saugus also had a freshman QB by the name of Mike DiChiaria who had a breakout season.

Broderick’s option offense helped Saugus put together back-to-back 7–3 seasons. The 2007 team, the first winning side since 1997, averaged 280 rushing yards per game according to the Item. Captain Tyler Trainor made 108 tackles and returned an interception for a touchdown. Saugus won its last three on the road, closing with a 49–14 Thanksgiving win at Chelsea. In 2008, Mike Dean rushed for 1,242 yards on 130 carries and quarterback Brett Reid added 800 on 96. After a three-game skid, the Sachems beat Danvers, Marblehead and Chelsea by a combined 92–13.

From 2009 through 2011, the Sachems fell back to below .500. Although these teams didn’t have as much success, they still had some All-Star players like Shamir Guillaume and AJ Guthro. Guillaume would go on to set the Sachems single season rushing yards record by rushing for 1,678 yards in 2010.

The Sachems finished 6–5 in 2012 and 3–8 in 2013. Tom Trainor, C.J. Randolph, Nick Benoit and Ismael Minaya are listed for 2012. Justin Winn earned Lynn Item All-Scholastic honors as a junior in 2013, when his newspaper profile credited him with 1,103 rushing yards and 19 touchdowns.

In 2014, Saugus finished 6–5. Dan Cacciola’s 375-yard, four-touchdown game against Winthrop surpassed Mike Nicolo’s earlier 306-yard single-game mark. The statistics table records 1,467 rushing yards and 18 rushing touchdowns for Cacciola, and 1,255 yards and 22 rushing touchdowns for Justin Winn. The archive describes Winn’s 22 rushing touchdowns as a school record. Cacciola’s surname appears as Cicciola in parts of the supplied workbook; the gallery and statistics section use Cacciola.

Saugus finished 3–9–1 in 2015 and 1–10 in 2016, as listed in the season archive. Brendan Grocki and Cam Williamson appear among the notable players for those teams. Mike Broderick’s tenure ended after the 2016 season, concluding twelve seasons as head coach.
2017 onward: Nalen, Mabee, Cummings and Bluestein
Anthony Nalen (2017)

Anthony Nalen was hired in 2017, and Saugus improved from the previous season. Ricky Martinez helped lead the Sachems. Unfortunately, due to a controversy during the 2018 off-season, Nalen was removed as head coach.
Mike Mabee (2018)

After Nalen’s departure, former Sachems great and former player under Coach Ginolfi, Mike Mabee, was hired to serve as interim Head Coach. Coach Mabee was able to guide a competitive team to a 4-7 record. The team was led by All-Star Dante McGrane.
Steve Cummings (2019–2025)

The Sachems under Coach Cummings have seen their ups and downs. The Sachems took a step back during the 2019 season when they went 3-8. The team was led by All Star Marvens Jean as well as Kyle Surette, Sal Franco, Christian Correa, and Javier Martinez.
The 2020 Season was interrupted by the Covid-19 Pandemic, but Saugus was still able to play a 7 game schedule during the season, going 2-5.
Saugus finished 0–11 in 2021 and 2–11 in 2022. Mike MacEacheran and Braden Faiella were among the players from those seasons.

The 2023 Sachems finished 5–6. Braden Faiella, Tommy DeSimmone and Dylan Clark are listed among the season’s leading players. The gallery’s senior Faiella profile reports 140 tackles and a career total of 482, and credits him with Item Defensive Player of the Year recognition. The coach’s suggestion that the career total might be a state record is not treated as a verified record. The supplied workbook also spells his first name Brandon.
The 2024 Sachems went 3-8 and were led by All Stars Koby Jette and Cody Munafo.

Steve Cummings’s final team finished 2–9 in 2025, beating Lynn Vo-Tech and East Boston. Saugus shut out East Boston 34–0, then took a 20–0 lead five minutes into its Thanksgiving game at Peabody. A blocked punt recovered in the end zone helped build the lead. Peabody rallied to win 28–26.
Greg Bluestein (2026–present)

Greg Bluestein, a 2008 Saugus graduate, returned to the staff in 2022 and served as defensive coordinator and associate head coach before succeeding Steve Cummings in February 2026. Roster shortages forced the Sachems to forfeit two October games. They returned to play at Arlington Catholic, then earned Bluestein’s first win as head coach, 24–20 at O’Bryant on November 13. The season record stood at 1–9 through that game.
Conclusion

The archive spans an era when a coach could arrange an extra game to influence the state standings, the years when a berth at Manning Bowl brought two communities together, and the modern conference and playoff schedules. The Thanksgiving scores trace another part of that history, from the early meetings with Watertown and Danvers to the games against Chelsea and Peabody. A surviving box score can still restore a name to a decisive play or explain a result that the standings alone cannot.
